summary: For ages 12–13: build two coupled ideas about supervolcanoes — (1) the NON-LINEAR scale gap between an ordinary eruption and a VEI-8 supereruption (thousands of km³ vs <1 km³, a collapse caldera rather than a cone), and (2) the causal CLIMATE CHAIN by which sulphur dioxide injected into the stratosphere forms sulphate aerosols that scatter sunlight and cause a multi-year 'volcanic winter' that then recovers. Learners should attribute the cooling to stratospheric sulphate aerosols — not ash, not CO2 — and treat the Toba bottleneck hypothesis as contested science. Anchored by the historical 1815 Tambora / 1816 'year without a summer' analogue and framed by MS-ESS2-2's gradual-processes-punctuated-by-catastrophe idea.
misconceptions: 'A supervolcano is just a bigger normal volcano.' — It is orders of magnitude larger (VEI 8), erupts from a huge shallow magma chamber, and leaves a collapse caldera rather than a cone; the difference is non-linear, not incremental.
'The global cooling comes from ash blocking the sun.' — Ash falls out within days–weeks; the years-long cooling is caused by sulphate AEROSOLS from SO2 in the stratosphere scattering sunlight.
'Volcanoes mainly warm the climate (CO2).' — On short timescales the dominant climate effect of a big eruption is COOLING via sulphate aerosols; volcanic CO2 is small compared with human emissions.
'Yellowstone is overdue and will definitely erupt soon.' — 'Overdue' misreads recurrence intervals (long-run averages, not schedules); a supereruption is very low-probability in any given year.
'The aerosols and cooling last a long time / permanently.' — Stratospheric sulphate aerosols persist for a few years then settle out; the climate recovers — the winter is severe but temporary.
'The Toba bottleneck is a proven fact.' — It is a debated hypothesis; genetic and archaeological evidence is mixed — a good example of contested science, not settled history.

activities.title: Turn the eruption dial: from cone to caldera on a log scale
steps: Work with an eruption-size control (a dial or slider) whose erupted-volume axis is drawn as a LOG scale, and record what the volcano looks like at ordinary scales versus when pushed toward VEI 8.
Notice and describe the structural change at the top end: the mountain does not simply grow taller — the emptied magma chamber collapses into a broad caldera tens of kilometres across.

Compare an ordinary eruption (<1 km³) against a supereruption (thousands of km³) using a side-by-side 'ghost' reference, and state in your own words how many times bigger it is, not just 'a bit bigger'.

Write one sentence explaining why each step up the VEI scale (from about VEI 2 upward) means roughly ten times more material, so a VEI-8 eruption like Toba or Yellowstone's largest is thousands of times (or more) bigger than an ordinary eruption.
activities.insight: A supervolcano is not an ordinary volcano scaled up a little; erupted volume differs by orders of magnitude (a logarithmic scale), and the structural signature is a collapse caldera, not a built-up cone.

activities.title: Build the volcanic-winter causal chain
steps: Assemble, in order, the causal sequence as an explicit chain: dissolved SO2 in the magma → blasted high into the STRATOSPHERE → forms sulphate aerosols → scatter/reflect incoming sunlight → global surface cooling for a year or two → recovery.

Using linked panels (an aerosol-spread world map and a global temperature-anomaly graph that respond together), observe how a stratospheric injection blooms a pale aerosol veil across the globe and drives the temperature graph into a multi-year dip that then recovers.
Run two contrasts: turn the SO2 amount down and watch the cooling weaken or vanish; keep the plume LOW (tropospheric only) and watch the aerosols rain out locally with no global winter.

State explicitly which ingredient caused the cooling and why ash and CO2 did not: ash falls out within days to weeks and only regionally; eruption CO2 is small and warms only slightly over long timescales.
activities.insight: The years-long global cooling is caused by sulphate aerosols formed from SO2 that must reach the stratosphere to persist and spread worldwide — the cooling is severe but temporary, and is not due to ash or CO2.

activities.title: Calibrate on Tambora, then scale up to Toba and Yellowstone
steps: Study the 1815 Tambora eruption and the 1816 'year without a summer' as a real, labelled data point on the temperature-anomaly graph, and describe the Northern-Hemisphere cooling and crop failures that followed.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Volcanoes pour out ash, CO2 and sulphur dioxide — which of these cooled the planet after Tambora, and how did it cool rather than warm?' Give both the agent and the reason.

Scale the reasoning up from Tambora to Toba (~74 ka) and Yellowstone, describing how a much larger supereruption could reach up and cool the entire planet, and connect this to how a cooling pulse could interact with an ice age (snow and ice reflecting still more sunlight).

Tackle the transfer counterexamples: why a typical Hawaiian-style lava eruption usually has little global cooling effect even when it produces a lot of lava, compared with a smaller explosive eruption that blasts SO2 into the stratosphere; and why a factory and a supervolcano emitting the same CO2 would differ in short-term effect.
activities.insight: A smaller historical analogue makes the abstract climate forcing concrete and transferable; the same mechanism scaled up explains how a rare supereruption can be a planet-wide catastrophic punctuation.

activities.title: Weigh the Toba bottleneck as contested science
steps: Take on the role of a volcanologist or climate scientist and debate the question 'Is the Toba catastrophe / human genetic bottleneck real?', laying out evidence for and against.

Separate what is well-supported (the eruption's scale and the aerosol-cooling mechanism) from what is debated (whether it caused a human population bottleneck ~74 ka), citing the mixed genetic and archaeological picture.
Discuss why 'Yellowstone is overdue' is a misreading: recurrence intervals are long-run averages, not schedules, and a supereruption is very low-probability in any given year.
Conclude with a short written statement distinguishing a dramatic-but-debated hypothesis from settled fact, and how scientists weigh such claims.
activities.insight: Science distinguishes robust mechanisms from contested historical inferences; the Toba bottleneck is a genuine, debated hypothesis, and 'overdue' misreads probability.

activities.title: Check the key discriminations
steps: After building the mechanism, answer short items that discriminate the cooling agent: choose sulphate aerosols (not ash, not CO2) as the cause of multi-year global cooling and justify the choice.
Put the causal-chain steps into the correct order and match the caldera to the supereruption and the cone to an ordinary eruption.
Explain why plume height into the stratosphere matters, and correct the statement 'Yellowstone is overdue so it will erupt soon.'
activities.insight: Learners can reliably distinguish the real cooling mechanism and the structural/scale signatures from common distractors.

checkQuestion: After the 1815 Tambora eruption, 1816 became 'the year without a summer' and crops failed across the Northern Hemisphere. Volcanoes pour out ash, CO2 and sulphur dioxide. Which of these cooled the planet, and how did it cool it rather than warm it?
checkAnswer: Sulphur dioxide did it. SO2 injected into the stratosphere reacts to form tiny sulphate aerosol droplets that spread around the globe and reflect/scatter incoming sunlight back to space, cooling the surface for a year or two. Ash falls out within days to weeks (too heavy to linger and only regional), and although CO2 is a warming gas the amount from even a giant eruption is small next to the aerosol cooling — so the short-term net effect is cooling.
